utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Ohaio gozaimas."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I wish I could say it in Korean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President. I would just like to introduce to the Trial Chamber Aleksandar Tesic, who is joining us from Republika Srpska. He is an intern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. May I also introduce Veronika Miteva, who is from Bulgaria and who has been assisting my team for the last four months. She'll be graduating this summer from The Hague University of applied sciences. "Ohaio gozaimas."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Excellency Akashi.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you whether you met somebody from the international organisations, particularly UNHCR, on 11th of July, 1995, and whether they informed you about what the population from Srebrenica wanted to be done?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just consult with my appointment book. My appointment book for July 11th 1995, does not indicate that I met with a representative of UNHCR on that day, but as everybody knows, that was an extremely busy day, and I met with many people. I had to make some crucial phone calls to New York and to the minister of defence of Holland, and the lack of mentioning UNHCR does not mean that I did not have this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have D1039 in the courtroom. Probably it will remind you on your report to Annan and Gharekhan.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may ask, would it be possible to, when the document's displayed, slowly scroll down through the document to give the Ambassador an opportunity to look at the document rather than just the header.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can also give him this in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Would you like the Ambassador to read through the document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It's not necessary, but I would like him to take a look. So if we can give him a hard copy would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we printed it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, may I ask you to see second page, paragraph (b). You may be right, it doesn't mean that it had to be a meeting.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have -- you have had some impressions that at the beginning, representatives of the Bosnian government were reluctant to support the evacuation of the civilians. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And for the participants, this is in Exhibit P5197. 5197.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, Excellency, it seems that the government finally agreed that the Serbs be solicited to allow all residents who want to leave -- who wish to leave enclave. Do you agree, and do you see that in this report of yours?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the question of the safe departure of those residents of Srebrenica who wished to do so was a very hot controversial issue between UNPROFOR and the Bosnian government. Bosnian government was taking the position that those residents should in principle stay in Srebrenica, and UNHCR took the position for humanitarian reasons that those of the residents who wished to leave the enclave should be allowed to do so. So there was a very prolonged difficult negotiations, and, of course, UNPROFOR supported UNHCR in its position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. And if you -- if you wish, you could review the whole document, but ...

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think for the convenience of all those present here, probably I'd like to ask Dr. Karadzic to draw our attention to any particular passage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have number -- page 3, please, next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, do you remember under point 3 you reported to New York what the UNHCR will do? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was it first provision of emergency, food, and medicine, number: "(ii) safe, rapid, and order early departure from Srebrenica of all those people, including men of military age, for Tuzla, beginning with the evacuation of wounded on an emergency basis."

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you estimated in the next sentence that it will be a massive logistic operation?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did, according to your memories, Serb side responded concerning rapid -- safe, rapid, and orderly departure from Srebrenica? You envisaged that it was going to commence 13th, but it seemed to me that it was accomplished by 13th in the morning hours.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the UNHCR and UNPROFOR contact Serb side, and was -- what was the response and co-operation of the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was UNHCR which was talking with the Bosnian Serb side, and I do not specifically recall what was the Serb response to UNHCR proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. Did you propose on 12th of July, did you propose to the Security Council content or elements of the resolution on the situation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you describe the thrust of this resolution? It's a draft resolution, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have D03401.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your communication to Mr. Annan, Gharekhan, and Stoltenberg on 12th of July - do you remember, Excellency? - and there is your signature.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not recall this cable specifically. I'd like to see a copy of it if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We may offer this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll print out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to take -- to see the three last paragraph on the first page. Before number (1 ), "We understand, not only from your cable ...," and so on. And then paragraph (2) that you suggested for this draft Security Council resolution to comprise the text there: "... according to UNHCR a great majority of the residents of Srebrenica do not wish to remain there. They are already displaced persons from elsewhere and will wish to move on."

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think this coincides very much with my impressions with the situation in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you mentioned that you noticed the relationship between the military and civilian authorities of the Republika Srpska were unusual or disturbed or so. Did you have a meeting on 17th of July in Belgrade with President Milosevic and General Mladic, and was it unusual for you that President Milosevic wanted to by-pass me and recommend General Mladic as a partner to the international -- internationals, and did you report the UN about your observation?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Dr. Karadzic. Did you mention 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. The cable could be 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I think you probably meant a meeting at one of the villas of President Milosevic which was held on the 15th of July where General Mladic suddenly appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think you are right, Excellency, but it could have been 16th too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court 1D25500.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If my memory serves me, it took place on the 15th, and I was aware of the meeting, and some of the participants I knew rather well. And I remember my impression of General Mladic on that day was that he was -- he was under very tense pressures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Can we have page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, in the first paragraph on this page, sixth line from the top, it says: "We would then play into the hands of Milosevic, who has long wanted us to believe that --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's make sure whether Ambassador is following.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 2 of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you have the hard copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm wondering whether Dr. Karadzic is referring to a cable which I sent to New York dated 12 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to have it in hard copy as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At first paragraph on front page, Excellency, it said that "yesterday," "called on me yesterday to discuss the situation," or maybe -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What paragraph are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like you to see the second page, and first paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Karadzic is referring to paragraph 3, which starts from the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Now I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the first page is says that Portillo seemed intrigued over the fact that the Bosnian Serbs did not mention Karadzic in the talks yesterday. And then it said that: "We would then play into the hands of Milosevic who has long wanted us to believe that this leader is a more co-operative Serb leader than Karadzic ..."

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was your impression and conclusion, Excellency, about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But shall we first find out what this single leader or this leader in this paragraph means, who it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, can you help us? Who was the leader that President Milosevic preferred or proposed to you as the one more co-operative with whom you should co-operate further?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess from the context that two people are particularly referred to in this paragraph. One is Dr. Karadzic as a civilian leader, and the other is General Mladic as the military leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the issue that you have noticed as unusual and unpleasant? What President Milosevic preferred?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think our discussions with the newly appointed British Secretary of State for Defence in this particular passage is sort of thinking aloud, somewhat speculative on the internal differences in the Bosnian Serb leadership. And I can think of reason why Dr. Karadzic wants us to pay special attention to this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you notice what President Milosevic would like to -- whom President Milosevic would like to be your partner on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think here again the discussions at this meeting are somewhat speculative, and I'm referred to as cautioning speculation with regard to something we do not know directly, but I think the absence of Dr. Karadzic from the meeting hosted by President Milosevic at his villa on the 15th of July, absence of Dr. Karadzic, gave rise to some speculations in this regard, but I think we do not -- we did not at that time have any solid proof as to what was taking place. We were speculating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. And did you perceive this as a sensitive to have presence of General Mladic at the meeting of what Karadzic was not -- apparently not informed?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you reiterate your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Maybe I should ask to see P2279, another cable of yours of 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I have a copy of it if I may.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: This is Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, Mr. President, this cable refers to the presence of General Mladic at the meeting at the request of Bildt, meaning Mr. Carl Bildt. So it's not President Milosevic who selected General Mladic, but he was accommodating Carl Bildt's requests or wishes in this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Can we see the entire first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, I would ask you to see the sentence: "In view of the highly sensitive nature of the presence of Mladic at the meeting, it was agreed by all participants that this fact should not be mentioned at all in public."

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was sensitive about that, and ...

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I surmised that the role played by General Mladic around the situation in Srebrenica gave rise to all kinds of press speculations and that's why I think it was agreed that the presence of Mladic should not be mentioned in public, but this is my guess only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. Due to the lack of time, I skipped many subjects and many of your documents, but I do hope I will have another opportunity to tender it. Thank you very much for coming and testifying. I don't have any questions at that moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in this connection, in my booklet I make a short reference to the atmosphere of that meeting and what I perceived to be the psychological mood of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have a page number, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please just give me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. In the meantime, Mr. Karadzic, I take it you are tendering 1D25500.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Excellency. This is the only one that is not admitted so far this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D3512, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm now able to identify a particular paragraph in my booklet referring to that meeting and the behaviour of General Mladic in addition to the presence of Rupert Smith. That's on page 85, the last paragraph, starting with, "Several days after the Srebrenica massacre."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If parties do not oppose, the Chamber is minded to admit this page. Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be added to the exhibit. Very well. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And before I begin, Your Honours, I should just tell you, I made my estimate yesterday in rough anticipation of what I thought might transpire today with the examination-in-chief, and hearing what I've just heard in the last hour, I've revised my cross-examination estimate and I think it will be less than I had indicated to Your Honours yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yesterday in your testimony to Dr. Karadzic, at transcript pages 37687 to 37688, you roughly outlined some of the findings of the United Nations expert commission that you convened to investigate the marketplace killings in February 1994 in Sarajevo. And just to be sure, can I take it that when you referred to their conclusions you did that actually from a distance, so to speak, not having had an opportunity to review their report before you gave evidence yesterday? A distance, so to speak, of about 18 years?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And at that time, in 1994 as well as presently, Mr. Ambassador, can I also take it that you have no knowledge of any local or other investigations that might have been conducted into the incident?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that subsequent to the investigation conducted by our expert commission?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Any at all.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any at all. I'm not aware of. I'm aware of a lot of speculations prior to and subsequent to the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, still on the subject of this incident yesterday at transcript pages 37694, Dr. Karadzic showed you a document. It has the number -- the exhibit number D717. So we could call that up, and I can also give you a hard copy of that document. And for the record, it's an outgoing code cable from you to Mr. Annan, number Z-1256, dated 16 August 1994, regarding the weapons collection points in Sarajevo, and it attaches two other documents to it. Now, the first document it attaches is the signed points of agreement between you and Dr. Karadzic, dated 18 February 1994. And again for the record that points of agreement document is also P1654 and P183 -- pardon me, P1820. And the second is this -- an unsigned protocol of understanding with the typewritten date at the bottom being 19 February 1994 and typewritten notation --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry. If my friend with the e-court document could go to the points of agreement which is the second attachment to this cable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Page 3. And then the unsigned protocol of understanding is page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the unsigned protocol of understanding has the place written as being Lukavica. And yesterday, Dr. Karadzic asked you if you saw the number 1 in this protocol which he said: "Regulates their right to self-defence in the case of the withdrawal of the UNPROFOR from the interposition areas and in the case --" pardon me, "And in the case --" yes. Page 4, please, in e-court: "And in the case that UNPROFOR is not able either to prevent or stop attack, the Serbs reserve the right to implement adequate measures of self-defence." And you confirmed yesterday that you saw this, and you may recall in moving on to another document I stood and raised a query, and Dr. Karadzic said, "I believe it was not that Excellency Akashi have seen it but that he participated in concluding this." So this is still the preface to the question, and I'd just like to show you before I ask you the question another related document. It's P2188. I have a hard copy for you and it's code cable dated 12 September 1994, from your office to Mr. Annan, forwarding a report and a copy of the letter of UNPROFOR's senior legal advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's 2118.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you've had a chance, Mr. Ambassador, to have a look at this second related document, I'll ask you a question. But as you read, I'll make a couple of points about this second related document, P2118. The second paragraph on page 1 says: "Our review of negotiations has validated the first attachment to our Z-1256, entitled 'points of agreement.' The attached protocol, in contrast, is a Bosnian Serb proposal that was never accepted by us." And then the third paragraph continues that UN records indicate that the Serbs during discussions with you and other UNPROFOR members on the 18th of February express concern for their own security after the withdrawal of regrouping -- and regrouping, pardon me, of heavy weapons. "Rather than entering into any written agreement, UNPROFOR only noted their concerns and gave assurances that UNPROFOR units would be interpositioned between the two sides along confrontation lines. The Bosnian Serb side nevertheless reserved its right to take adequate measures of self-defence in case of attack by the other side. We did not endorse their position." Now, if we can go over to page 2 of this document and go down, thank you, to paragraph 4, page 2 being the legal memorandum. Paragraph 4 reads: "From the available information, I have found that the 'Protocol of Understanding' was a draft that had been prepared and submitted by the Bosnian Serb negotiators, but was found unacceptable by the UNPROFOR negotiators and never signed. And accordingly, it cannot be regarded as having any legal standing." Now, if you had a chance to review those documents, Mr. Ambassador, I'd like to ask you just two questions about them, if I may.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How -- first, can you put the documents in context, and second, how do they relate to one another?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: How ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do they relate to one another?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point I fail to understand the relationship.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll ask you the question in a different way then. Dr. Karadzic in his comments yesterday asserted to you that this additional protocol, which he said provided or allowed the Serbs a right to remove heavy weapons from the weapons collection points in case of attack, was concluded, and that was agreement between UNPROFOR and the Bosnian Serbs. These two documents together, Mr. Ambassador, would tend to show that contrary to what Dr. Karadzic observed, this protocol was, in fact, never concluded; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I think copies of these messages I sent to New York headquarters seemed to endorse what you have concluded from it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And to your mind there was no understanding that the Serbs or the Bosnians, for that matter, had a right to withdraw their weapons from weapon collections points under the terms of the agreement in the case of attack.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a military expert, but the fact that the presence of 20 to 30 UNPROFOR troops at each weapons collection point seemed to assume that their presence, presence of these UNPROFOR soldiers, was deemed necessary to meet with any eventuality, and I recall that Serbs wanted more weapons collection points and perhaps expected that lesser numbers will be present in case the number of such collection points were more numerous. I ventured a guess that one of the reasons for some disagreements between UNPROFOR Bosnian sector and NATO was due to NATO's misgivings, slight misgivings about the style of negotiation by General Michael Rose, and Michael Rose was a very able, great, very skilled negotiator. He tended to overwhelm his negotiating adversary by mastering impromptu arguments, and so he may have accepted at one point or another about this right of recovery of weapons once collected by the UN, but upon second thought, maybe he felt that UN should not specifically recognise this right. The right of self-defence always can be expanded in the mind of some of the parties concerned. That's why we have to be very cautious about sort of a liberal interpretation of the right of self-defence. So in the process of negotiations, always there are gives and takes, and upon reflection, any party, after consultation with their legal advisors, may alter the position they temporarily took in the course of negotiations and come to the conclusion that final document should not be signed or endorsed. So I could surmise that this incident may have been a product of these fluidities of negotiation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'll go on to another area, and it relates to something that we saw in your booklet, which is 65 ter number 1D29269, at page 80; that would be e-court page 43. And there you said: "Karadzic, as a negotiator, had the tenancy to twist the truth rather nonchalantly," a trait you observed not a few times. Your indulgence for a moment. Yes, it's at the bottom left-hand corner of the image on the screen in front of us. And then you gave two examples of that, both arising in the context of the Gorazde crisis. You said at the time -- at that time, Dr. Karadzic insisted that he had not received a fax from you concerning the UN officers taken hostage by his forces, and while many of them still remained hostage, he insisted that they had all been released, but you easily found out that that was not the case. And at -- if we can go over on the e-court image to the next page, very top: "At one time during Geneva negotiations in Gorazde, Karadzic made a strong statement that the Bosnian Serb forces under his command had withdrawn from a certain area, but on inspection by the UN on the spot, it turned out not true at all." So is this, Mr. Ambassador, what you were referring to yesterday when you spoke of your regret when during the Gorazde crisis Dr. Karadzic told you things his side was doing or hadn't done but on checking with UNPROFOR you found discrepancies in that regard?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, madam. That's very correct, and in fact, I recall that during the first ipso you referred to in this first paragraph of my booklet, some of my staff who were with me in the negotiation at Pale told me that we should leave the meeting in view of this clear discrepancy between what was told to us by Dr. Karadzic and what we had subsequently confirmed from the ground. I -- I said no. I like to be courteous, and it would be very impolite to withdraw from a meeting which is too dramatic, and I stayed home, hoping in the meantime that more UNPROFOR hostages might be released. So I always wanted to give a benefit of doubt, and I recall Mr. Churkin, the Special Envoy of the Russian government who went with me to Pale. He was very disappointed and upset in the talks, and he decided to leave the meeting, and I stayed on. But I decided not to accept the invitation of my host to stay for dinner.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you noted that you had observed this trait of twisting the truth a few times, and I wonder if you could tell us as a consequence of this. What kind of weight did you give to any undertakings, representations, or agreements entered into by Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I came to know these tendencies, I was of course made more cautious, and I became, as time went on, much more cautious. I remember much later in those years of 1994 and 1995, in fact, yes, I think in conjunction with full-scale NATO air action in the latter part of August and beginning of September 1995, I paid a visit to President Milosevic, and I told him it is my distinct impression that NATO was preparing for full-scale air action. Therefore, it would be important that Serb side should be well aware of this determine -- strong, firm, determination by NATO and take that fact into account in their negotiations. Mr. Milosevic told me that he told this to Bosnian Serb leadership, Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic, and he said they laughed at Milosevic for conveying this warning which I had made. So there were misjudgements here and there, and I'd like to refer to my paragraph subsequent -- immediately after what you have quoted, and I quote: "I thought that the word promise or agreement might not carry as much weight on the Balkan Peninsula as in East Asia. According to certain informed sources, this practice goes back to the times of Ottoman Turkish rule, when as soon as the ruled concluded an agreement with the rulers, there is a contrive to live free from the constraints of the agreement." Here I am being theoretical and speculative and I don't mean this as an insult to Balkan culture, but I thought that the complex history of the Balkans might partly explain the weight we give to promises and agreements.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Part of the caution you treated his -- Dr. Karadzic's assertions and representations with, I assume, would have involved your checking with your staff and UNPROFOR units on the ground to determine, or be able to, so that you could assess the veracity of what you were being told; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To move on to another area but at the same period of time, yesterday, and that would be April 1994, yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Would you like us to add these pages to the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me. And because I had read portions of them out and Mr. Akashi had read a quote out, I thought initially not, but it would probably be best so that you can have the context of any remarks made to have those pages added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At this point the Chamber is minded to admit the whole chapter, i.e., chapter 4, emotional nationalist, Karadzic and Mladic, pages 77 to 85. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't have any problem with that, but I think it would even be better if -- this is a booklet, as Mr. Akashi has said, and it's not very long, so we really would appreciate if you could admit the whole thing under these circumstances. There are other chapters dealing with Izetbegovic, Tudjman, and I think it gives the context better if then taking one chapter dealing only with Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is not consistent with our practice. Then to be consistent we will admit only those two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just note that we have, although that's -- you are correct about our practice. There have been times that we have admitted entire documents such as the Assembly sessions that give a context to the events in general. I think this comes from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Sorry to interrupt you, but let us visit the issue at the end of his -- Mr. Akashi's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So as I said, just to move on to another area but staying at the same time period, April 1994, Dr. Karadzic showed you yesterday at transcript page 37686, a copy of your correspondence with Mr. Annan reporting on your meetings with him on the 7th of April, and that's D3492. And I've just found a copy of it if you'd like to have a look at the whole document, Mr. Ambassador. Now, in the context of the discussion about this document, Dr. Karadzic referred you to 14, which is on the last page of the document, which relates to the question of your visit to -- or which related to in the discussions yesterday the question of your visit to Banja Luka, and I'd like to ask you about that. Your intention to visit the area arose in response to allegations of ethnic cleansing and violations of human rights in Banja Luka, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And yesterday, you said that to your frustration, although you raised the prospect of a visit with Dr. Karadzic a number of times and he said he was doing his best to facilitate it, the visit never happened. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Karadzic, I think, told us yesterday that he was concerned with my own safety, but -- because I had no means of ascertaining that my life was at risk. I always was accompanied by my bodyguards, and so I thought my being in personal danger is a little bit hard for me to conceive. I was faced with similar dangers a number of times in my life, and that's part of my job.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another document relating to Banja Luka, jumping forward in time from April 1994 to September of that year. Your indulgence for a moment. If we could have a look, please, at P5423, and it's a copy of a letter, a letter that you wrote to Dr. Karadzic on 20 September 1994. And if we could go over to page 2 of the document on the screen. And I have a hard copy, Mr. Ambassador, if you'd like to have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this letter to Dr. Karadzic is a very strongly worded communication from you, conveying your utter dismay to him at the fact that in the past few days alone, over 2.500 Muslim civilians had been forcefully expelled from the area of Bijeljina and Janja. You noted that departures of non-Serb population of the area have been continuing, referring to 700 people arriving in Central Bosnia on 17 September 1994, and you recalled to Dr. Karadzic assurances he gave you on 20 August that such forceful expulsions of non-Serb population are not in accordance with the policies of Bosnian Serb authorities. The letter also shows that you had a telephone conversation with him on 6 September, and you informed -- he informed you that he had taken measures to identify, arrest, and prosecute those responsible for inhumane -- the inhumane and criminal expulsions of non-Serb civilians. You also reminded him that he gave the same assurance to Mr. Vieira de Mello, one of your staff, earlier that month, and you conclude in the last paragraph by telling Dr. Karadzic that you failed to understand how such a deplorable situation can continue and accelerate despite all the commitments he had made to you to stop the forceful expulsions and to improve conditions for the non-Serb population. And you notified him that those responsible for such acts would, of course, be subject to investigation and prosecution by this Tribunal. Mr. Akashi, would you like to comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this letter requires no additional explanation. This was a product of my utter dismay with the practice in -- in the area of Banja Luka, and I had no other alternative than writing this kind of straightforward letter from time to time to Dr. Karadzic. But I was accused, I remind you, of being over polite to Dr. Karadzic, and the well-known representative of a certain big power got hold of a copy of one of those polite letters which I sent to Dr. Karadzic and accused me of unduly polite and courteous. But I tried to be -- to do my best to maintain a trustful relationship with all my negotiating partners in three different parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It must have taken enormous energy as well as obvious commitment and dedication. I'd like to ask you some more questions about some of your assertions to Dr. Karadzic in this document. Is it at all feasible in your view that such large-scale population movements, 2.500 on the one hand, and 700 on the other hand, could take place, actually such large-scale and protracted population movements, because we have here incidents in September and you recall that yesterday you discussed your concerns over forced expulsions in Banja Luka in April. So is it at all feasible that movements of this type over such a protracted period could take place without, in your view, government knowledge and acquiescence?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "government"?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: State authorities.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean state authorities of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is most unlikely that this could take place without the knowledge of whichever local or autonomous authority in a country.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And once an area is emptied of all other ethnic groups -- actually, this kind of exercise, these expulsions, would you agree with me that they effectively by emptying the area of all its other ethnic groups create facts on the ground that would be very hard to reverse in a political negotiated settlement?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hard to reverse, yes, but if it is totally unjust and unforgiveable to bring about such population movement should not lead us to conclude that since reversal would be unrealistic, we have to accept the new situation which has been created as a result of whatever unlawful action. So I think difficulty with implementation is a different matter from whether it is lawful or rightful.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's 10.29. Would this be a good time to pause?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We're joined by Milos Bacic of Republika Srpska, who is also serving as an intern with our team. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, yesterday Dr. Karadzic showed you a document that now has the number D3495, and if we could have that on the screen. It's a copy of a response he made to you on your protest over an attack on a humanitarian convoy, and it's on the screen in front of you now. If we could go to page -- page 2 of this document, you'll see his response. Now, in this response, Dr. Karadzic writes: "I assure you that what took place cannot in any way be construed as representing the policy of the Republika Srpska, nor is the manner -- nor is this the manner in which the Army of the Republika Srpska behaves." Now, that was just to refresh your memory as to what you were shown yesterday. I'd like you now to have a look at P1686, and it's a letter of -- copy of a letter of protest from you to Dr. Karadzic on the 30th of July, 1994. Now, if we could just scroll down the page a little bit. The type script isn't the best, but in summary, this letter of yours to Dr. Karadzic refers to a report by the UNHCR chief of mission for Bosnia to Professor Koljevic, made on the 17th of July, of an incident on 18 June where sleeping bags and glue were confiscated at a Bosnian Serb check-point at Dobrun and another incident on 14 July where 500 bags of wheat flour were damaged. Beans were -- there was another incident on the 3rd of July when slashing of sacks of wheat flour again and beans caused damage, and then on 20 July the UNHCR Russian convoy reported that flour bags were again ripped and tins of meat were opened. Now, you pointed out to Dr. Karadzic that, "... all our convoys for Gorazde originate in Belgrade and travel exclusively through Serb-controlled areas ...," so you couldn't accept explanations for this loss of humanitarian goods as being necessary for security reasons. Now, it seems to me that the protest you made in this document and the behaviour that you brought to Dr. Karadzic's attention is exactly -- reflects behaviour that's contrary to Dr. Karadzic's assurances to you in his letter of March 24th as to how the Army of the Republika Srpska behaves. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is an instance of the lack of discipline in the armed forces of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your book, your booklet, you referred at page 26, which is e-court page 16, and still on the subject of humanitarian aid, you said at -- on page 26, the penultimate paragraph, you said: "From the view point of the parties in war, humanitarian assistance was not a disinterested moral action but an instrument to either weaken the position of their opponents or strengthen their own party, civilian as well as military." And you spoke in your book about statements made by the Bosnian authorities in that regard. But my question to you is: Isn't it the case, Mr. Ambassador, that you saw Dr. Karadzic and his military forces also interfere, particularly over the course of 1994 and 1995, with the distribution of humanitarian aid, using it as an instrument to weaken their opponents?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, it was a practice that both sides in this conflict, the Bosnian government as well as the Bosnian Serb forces, looked at humanitarian assistance as potentially aiding their side, or oppositely, as a means to strengthen their side. So they looked at what we considered to be purely a humanitarian act or action as something very political and militarily significant matter. We tried our best to dissuade parties to be concerned exclusively with their military balance, but often times it was our frustration that they continued to look at humanitarian activity from their own narrow partisan perspective.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could -- thank you. If we could just have a look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Ambassador, looking at this paragraph, it seems that this paragraph refers to the Bosnian government side, not the Bosnian Serb side. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The first sentence refers to the Bosnian government, but please look at the third sentence, "From the view point of the parties in war ..." So all the parties, without exception, unfortunately, looked at humanitarian assistance as interested assistance rather than disinterested assistance. That's very bad and unacceptable from a UN viewpoint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have, please, in e-court -- and perhaps before I go further I could ask for e-court page 16 of the Ambassador's book to be admitted. That's pages 26 and 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we look any passage on page 27, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We didn't. I only asked -- suggested page 27 because I actually don't know how to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In e-court that is on the same page. Yes. We'll add this page to the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. 65 ter 01291, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could, 65 ter number 01291, Mr. Ambassador, is dated 3 September 1994, and this is the cover page to your letter to Dr. Karadzic of that date. If we could go to the second page, please. It's a very smaller, so I think we can deal with it on the screen, but if you could enlarge that. Now, this letter that you wrote to Dr. Karadzic is -- expresses your concern about remarks you understand he made during a speech to his Assembly on the 1st of September, 1994, referring to economic sanctions imposed by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and said -- and he said that, "Now we have the full right to introduce such sanctions against Muslims so that even a bird will not fly through to them." And you urged him to refrain from taking any such action. Mr. Ambassador, is this reflective to your mind, the statements by Dr. Karadzic, reflective of the tendency of the parties to use humanitarian assistance perhaps as a lever rather than as disinterested assistance?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have that as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6293, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, one final question and one final issue, and it takes us back to your booklet, Mr. Ambassador, and so that's 65 ter number 1D29269, and it's at page 31 of the booklet, e-court pages 18 and 19, where you refer to the detention of UN personnel following the NATO air strikes in May of 1995. And I'd like to know whether you agree with me that UN personnel who were taken hostage on that occasion were used, actually, as human shields in order to compel NATO forces to stop the air strikes.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the term "human shield" is frequently used by journalism, but in this particular case, I think if we construe Bosnian Serb action of taking UNPROFOR personnel as a -- as hostage, if this act is construed as taking hostages and making them as human shield is certainly not an exaggeration, journalistic exaggeration.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ambassador, I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, Excellency, except to thank Excellency Akashi for his effort to come and testify. No additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Since there are many pages after your first ruling, I wonder whether there is now new -- new justification to tender and admit the whole book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the issue and decided to leave it as it is. Unless my colleagues have a question for you, Ambassador Akashi, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. You do not have an easy task, and I wish you and all your colleagues on both sides best of luck. Our task in international affairs is never easy, and almost always thankless, so you deserve a deeper appreciation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Arigato gozaimas."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Arigato gozaimas."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well -- yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I guess we should have brought General Galic, but sorry about that. Mr. President, there is one issue I'd just like to address briefly, and that is that General Mladic has filed a request for leave to respond to our motion for subpoena and we have no objection to his filing a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you're not going to make any observation, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I do not have the motion or request before me, but I think it's fairly safe to note that it is granted. There are a few matters I'd like to deal with before we adjourn today. The first thing is related to the accused's request for postponement of testimony of Slavko Puhalic. The Chamber is seized of the accused's request for postponement of testimony of subpoenaed witness Slavko Puhalic filed on 24th of April, 2014 -- I'm sorry, 2013. The accused requests that the date of Mr. Puhalic's testimony be postponed from 7th of May, 2013, to 30th of August, 2013, based on scheduling issues and to place his testimony at the same time as other witnesses from the north-western municipalities. So in this regard, the Chamber would like to ask the Prosecution if it is minded to respond to this request. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, then the Chamber will issue its ruling on the request now. The Chamber recalls the subpoena it issued on the 20th of March, 2013, ordering Mr. Puhalic to appear before this Chamber to testify on the 7th of May, 2013, or another date and time to be notified. In light of the accused's submission and the Prosecution's response, the Chamber considers that the postponement of Mr. Puhalic's testimony is warranted. The Chamber thus grants the accused's request and orders that Mr. Puhalic shall testify in this case on the 30th of August, 2013. The Chamber instruction the Registry to communicate the change of date of his testimony to Mr. Puhalic and to take any further necessary steps to implement the Chamber's decision. Now the Chamber wishes to return to the matter of the motion for the temporary transfer of detained witness Franc Kos filed on the 4th of April, 2013. The Chamber recalls that on the 18th of April, 2013, in response to a Chamber inquiry regarding the motion, Mr. Robinson stated that the Defence was unable to make any definitive representation regarding the Rule 90 bis requirements because, in his submission, Bosnian authorities generally do not respond to the Defence absent a request from the Chamber. In his submission, it is for this reason that the Defence requested that the Chamber issue an invitation to the BiH authorities verifying that the Rule 90 bis requirements have been satisfied. The Chamber recalls, however, multiple instances where the Defence has successfully liaised with the BiH authorities and, furthermore, considers that it is incumbent upon the parties to show that the Rule 90 bis requirements have been satisfied. The Chamber thus instructs the Defence to make an inquiry to the BiH directly and keep the Chamber apprised of any response or lack thereof from the BiH. Finally, the Chamber notes that the Defence may be assisted by filing its letter to BiH on the record as it has done on previous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And now the Chamber refers to the Prosecution's submission with respect to the portions of Milorad Dodik's interview and testimony in the Brdjanin case which were referred to during his cross-examination and which are now being tendered. The Chamber has reviewed the excerpts which have been uploaded as 65 ter 24921 and 24924. The Chamber is not convinced that these extracts need to be admitted into order to understand the testimony of Milorad Dodik or in order to assess his credibility. The relevant portions from both his testimony and interview were quoted or referred to in a way that the Chamber can understand the essence of the witness's evidence and the points raised on cross-examination. The witness also repeatedly confirmed the content of what he said during his testimony in the Brdjanin case. The Chamber also notes that 51 pages of Mr. Dodik's testimony from the Brdjanin case are being tendered, but the number of specific pages referred to during cross-examination was far fewer. Accordingly, the Chamber will not admit 65 ter 24921 or 24924 at this stage. Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, there may be some kind of upload problem, Mr. President. If the Chamber was presented with 51 pages of testimony from the Brdjanin case, my recollection was that the total number of pages that we intended to provide to the Chamber in conformity with the previous practice was far fewer; in fact, less than half. So there seems to be some problem that may have misled the Chamber. We really did try to limit the submission to matters that were addressed, so maybe we can just start over, and I'm sorry for the confusion. I would have checked that personally but we've never had that problem in the past. So maybe if we can commence again, and I indeed can mention to the Court where the references were made if that's helpful, but I apologise for what appears to be a logistical misstep. But as I mentioned to Mr. Robinson before, the number of pages we were submitting was far fewer. I think he is aware of that so there seems to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for the information, Mr. Tieger, but the main reason for the Chamber's ruling was stated in the previous part and that that situation does not make a cause for the Chamber to change its position. Thank you. Finally, the Chamber will issue an oral ruling on the admission of 65 ter 24232, which was tendered by the Prosecution on 10th of April, 2013, during the cross-examination of Witness Soniboje Skiljevic. The Chamber notes that the document in question is a 129-pages "Verdict of the Appellate Panel" of the BiH court in the case against Radoje Lalovic and Soniboje Skiljevic dated 11th of July, 2011, which is referred to in paragraph 17 of the Soniboje Skiljevic's witness statement which was admitted in this case as Exhibit D3331. The Chamber notes that the parties seek the admission of the document in full. The Chamber is satisfied that -- I'm sorry. Having reviewed the parties' submissions in relation to the verdict, as well as the document itself, the Chamber finds that only the first 13 pages of the English version of the verdict, as well as paragraphs 71, 80, 98 to 101, 104, 105, 108 to 111, 118, 129, 151, 158, 174, 205, 216, 225, 226, and 262 should be admitted into evidence. The Chamber is satisfied that these paragraphs cover the questions raised in court during the cross-examination of the witness and show the outcome of the verdict, as well as the reasoning of the appellate panel in reaching such outcome. The Chamber hereby instructs the Prosecution to upload onto e-court the first 13 pages of the verdict as well as the 22 paragraphs just referred to. The Chamber further instructs the Registry to assign this redacted version of 65 ter 24232 an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That be Exhibit P6294, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, unless there's anything to be raised, the hearing is adjourned. The next hearing will be on 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of May, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.36 a.m.
